messages.content: I want mobile manipulators to reposition unseen furniture while maintaining contact. The central challenge is distinguishing object slip from localization drift. The goals are to reposition the furniture within 5 cm in 90% of trials despite intermittent visual occlusion, and to identify slip versus localization drift with 90% balanced accuracy without external tracking during execution.

That sets out two related requirements. The repositioning requirement concerns where the unseen furniture ends up: within 5 cm in 90% of trials, under intermittent visual occlusion. The identification requirement concerns whether the manipulator can distinguish object slip from localization drift, reaching 90% balanced accuracy without relying on external tracking during execution. Maintaining contact matters throughout the furniture-repositioning task, not just at the end.
Why is it important to distinguish slip from localization drift rather than just notice that something seems wrong?

They describe different kinds of discrepancy. Object slip concerns a change involving the object at the maintained contact; localization drift concerns an error in the manipulator's estimate of position. Either could make the apparent relationship between the manipulator and furniture seem inconsistent, but merely detecting an inconsistency would not establish which one occurred. The stated goal specifically requires identifying slip versus localization drift.
Does the goal say that the furniture has to remain visible the whole time?

No. It explicitly includes intermittent visual occlusion, so continuous visual access cannot be assumed. It does not specify when occlusion occurs, how long it lasts, or whether every view of the furniture is blocked at once. The 5 cm and 90%-of-trials requirement applies in the stated setting with intermittent visual occlusion.
And by unseen furniture, do we mean a particular furniture item that has already been described?

No particular item is specified. “Unseen furniture” is the condition given for the repositioning goal; the statement does not name a furniture category, list the objects, or define exactly what prior exposure is excluded. It is best to retain the wording rather than add a more specific familiarity condition.
I don't want the 5 cm figure confused with the classification score. Can you separate the two targets?

Certainly. “Within 5 cm in 90% of trials” is the furniture-repositioning target. “90% balanced accuracy” is the target for distinguishing object slip from localization drift. They use different measures: a distance tolerance and trial-success rate for repositioning, versus a classification metric for the slip-versus-drift distinction.
What exactly does balanced accuracy convey here?

For a two-class distinction, balanced accuracy is the average of the recall for the slip class and the recall for the localization-drift class. A target of 90% balanced accuracy is therefore not simply a target of 90% correct predictions overall. Nor does it, on its own, say that recall must be exactly 90% for each class individually.
Does that classification requirement allow an external system to track the furniture as the manipulator works?

The requirement expressly says “without external tracking during execution.” The slip-versus-localization-drift identification must meet its 90% balanced-accuracy target under that restriction. The wording does not otherwise specify which information sources the manipulator uses or how performance is assessed outside execution.
I also want to be clear about maintaining contact. Is it just a way of describing the setting, or part of the objective?

It is part of the stated goal: mobile manipulators are to distinguish object slip from localization drift while maintaining contact during furniture repositioning. The node does not give contact a separate numerical success threshold or specify how contact is measured, so it should not be turned into an invented third metric.
Could the system meet the goal by keeping contact and classifying correctly, even if the furniture finishes farther than 5 cm away?

Those observations would not by themselves satisfy the repositioning requirement. The goal also calls for unseen furniture to be repositioned within 5 cm in 90% of trials with intermittent visual occlusion. Classification performance, contact during repositioning, and final repositioning performance are connected aspects of the goal, but one does not replace the others.
Conversely, if the furniture ends up within 5 cm, is that enough to say the slip-versus-drift goal has been achieved?

No. The stated classification target is distinct: 90% balanced accuracy for identifying object slip versus localization drift, without external tracking during execution. A successful final position alone would not establish that the manipulator made that distinction accurately.
Does 90% of trials mean that every period of occlusion has to be handled successfully?

The stated percentage applies to trials in the repositioning requirement, not to individual periods of occlusion. Intermittent visual occlusion is a condition under which that requirement applies. The goal does not define a separate success rate for each occlusion period.
Is the 5 cm limit about how far the furniture is moved, or how close it gets to its intended placement?

It is a repositioning-accuracy target: the furniture is to be placed within 5 cm, rather than moved by only 5 cm. The statement does not give the intended placements or a more detailed distance-calculation convention, so those details should remain open.
Can we state what kind of manipulator or sensing arrangement is required?

The goal specifies mobile manipulators, maintaining contact, intermittent visual occlusion, and no external tracking during execution for the slip-versus-drift identification target. It does not prescribe a particular manipulator design, sensor set, or identification method. Those choices should not be presented as though they were already part of the requirement.
So how would you express the full goal in one careful sentence?

Enable mobile manipulators to distinguish object slip from localization drift while maintaining contact during furniture repositioning, with the aims of repositioning unseen furniture within 5 cm in 90% of trials under intermittent visual occlusion and identifying slip versus localization drift with 90% balanced accuracy without external tracking during execution.

For the furniture-repositioning goal, I propose fusing tactile shear, wheel–arm odometry, and intermittent RGB-D in a contact-anchored graph that estimates furniture pose, object slip, and localization drift.

That is a proposed way to make the three estimates jointly rather than treating each discrepancy in isolation. Tactile shear provides information at the contact, wheel–arm odometry provides information about the manipulator’s motion, and intermittent RGB-D provides visual and depth observations when available. The contact-anchored graph is the proposed framework for relating those observations to furniture pose, slip, and localization drift. This describes an approach, not a demonstrated result.
What does “contact-anchored” mean here? Does it mean we assume the furniture never slips?

No. Contact-anchored means the maintained contact is central to how the proposed graph relates the manipulator and furniture. It must not be read as an assumption that their relationship is perfectly fixed: object slip is explicitly one of the quantities the graph is meant to estimate.
Then why include both slip and localization drift as estimates?

Because the proposal is aimed at distinguishing them. A discrepancy between expected and observed motion need not have a single interpretation: it could involve motion at the object contact or error in localization. Estimating both allows the proposed graph to represent those possibilities separately, rather than calling any discrepancy “slip” or any discrepancy “drift.” Whether it can distinguish them reliably is not established by the proposal alone.
Is tactile shear supposed to settle that distinction by itself?

The proposal calls for fusion, not a decision based solely on tactile shear. Shear is relevant to what is happening at contact, but the proposed distinction also draws on wheel–arm odometry and whatever intermittent RGB-D observations are available. The node does not specify a rule under which a particular shear reading proves slip.
What does wheel–arm odometry contribute conceptually?

It contributes motion information associated with the mobile base and arm. In this proposal, that information can be considered alongside contact information and RGB-D observations when estimating furniture pose, slip, and localization drift. The proposal does not prescribe a particular odometry model or say that odometry is free of error.
And is RGB-D meant to be continuous visual tracking?

No. The proposal expressly says intermittent RGB-D. Its visual and depth observations would be available only intermittently, consistent with the goal’s intermittent visual occlusion. The graph is proposed to fuse those observations with tactile shear and wheel–arm odometry, rather than requiring an uninterrupted RGB-D view.
Does mentioning RGB-D contradict the requirement to work without external tracking during execution?

Not inherently. RGB-D observations and external tracking are not synonymous. The requirement rules out reliance on external tracking during execution for identifying slip versus localization drift; the proposal names intermittent RGB-D as an input but does not specify a camera placement or an external tracking system. It should not be expanded into a claim about hardware that has not been stated.
When you say “graph,” are particular factors or update equations already chosen?

No particular factors, equations, or update procedure are specified. “Contact-anchored graph” describes the proposed estimation structure at a high level: it relates the named information sources around the contact while estimating the named quantities. A detailed mathematical formulation would be an additional design choice, not a fact supplied here.
Could I simplify the proposal to estimating furniture pose from intermittent RGB-D?

That would leave out much of it. The proposal fuses three sources—tactile shear, wheel–arm odometry, and intermittent RGB-D—and estimates three things: furniture pose, slip, and localization drift. Its contact-anchored structure is also important, particularly because contact is maintained during repositioning and slip is one of the distinctions of interest.
Does “furniture pose” mean just whether the furniture reached the target location?

Not quite. Pose is an estimate of the furniture’s placement, rather than merely a yes-or-no success judgment. The separate goal specifies repositioning unseen furniture within 5 cm in 90% of trials under intermittent visual occlusion. This proposal names furniture-pose estimation as part of an approach that could be used toward that goal; it does not report that the threshold has been reached.
Should we say the graph will achieve 90% balanced accuracy on slip versus localization drift?

We should keep that as the goal, not as a proven property of the proposed graph. The required outcome is 90% balanced accuracy for identifying slip versus localization drift without external tracking during execution. The present proposal describes what information to fuse and what to estimate, but supplies no performance result.
Likewise, does this proposal establish that furniture can be repositioned within 5 cm in 90% of trials?

No. That remains the repositioning requirement, including the conditions of unseen furniture and intermittent visual occlusion. Estimating furniture pose in the proposed graph is relevant to it, but the proposal alone does not establish any trial success rate or final-placement accuracy.
Could the graph simply treat every apparent furniture movement as localization drift?

That would not express the proposal faithfully. It explicitly estimates both slip and localization drift, along with furniture pose. The point of representing them separately is to preserve the slip-versus-drift distinction rather than assigning every apparent movement to one category. The proposal does not, however, specify exactly how each case is resolved.
Is the contact anchor an external reference for true furniture position?

No external reference for true position is stated. “Contact-anchored” identifies how the proposed graph is organized around the manipulator–furniture contact; it does not turn that contact into ground-truth tracking. In particular, because slip is estimated, the proposal does not treat contact as an infallible fixed reference.
How much can we say about what happens during a visual occlusion?

We can say that RGB-D is intermittent and that the proposed fusion also includes tactile shear and wheel–arm odometry. We cannot infer a specified occlusion-handling algorithm, a maximum occlusion duration, or guaranteed accuracy while the view is unavailable. Those details are not part of the proposal.
So the short formulation is: use all three sources in a contact-anchored graph, while keeping pose, slip, and drift distinct?

Yes. More explicitly: propose fusing tactile shear, wheel–arm odometry, and intermittent RGB-D in a contact-anchored graph that estimates furniture pose, object slip, and localization drift. It is an approach to the maintained-contact repositioning goal and its slip-versus-drift distinction, not a claim that the stated accuracy targets have already been demonstrated.
During 3-second RGB-D occlusions, can contact-anchored fusion distinguish gripper–furniture slip from localization drift?

That is the question to resolve, not an established capability. The proposed fusion combines tactile shear, wheel–arm odometry, and intermittent RGB-D in a contact-anchored graph. During a 3-second RGB-D occlusion, it would have no new RGB-D observation from that occluded view, so the distinction would depend on what the remaining information can support. The proposal does not establish whether that is sufficient.
Why specify gripper–furniture slip here rather than just say the furniture moved?

“Gripper–furniture slip” makes the location of the possible relative motion explicit: it is at the contact between the gripper and the furniture. Apparent furniture motion alone would not tell us whether that contact slipped or the manipulator’s localization drifted. The question asks whether the fusion can tell those explanations apart during the 3-second occlusion.
Does maintaining contact rule out gripper–furniture slip?

No. Maintaining contact and having no slip are different claims. The gripper can remain in contact with the furniture while their relative position changes. That is why slip remains a quantity to distinguish from localization drift even in a contact-anchored approach.
What does the occlusion change about the question?

It limits the availability of RGB-D observations for 3 seconds. The proposed fusion includes intermittent RGB-D, but it cannot draw a new observation from an occluded RGB-D view during that interval. The question is whether tactile shear and wheel–arm odometry, considered within the contact-anchored graph, leave enough information to separate slip from drift until visual and depth information is available again.
Are you saying those two remaining sources definitely suffice for all 3 seconds?

No. Naming the available sources is not a sufficiency claim. The question supplies neither a result nor conditions that would establish reliable identification throughout a 3-second occlusion. It is entirely possible to pose the distinction without assuming the proposed fusion has already achieved it.
Could tactile shear by itself prove that the gripper slipped on the furniture?

The proposal does not give a rule that turns a tactile-shear observation into proof of slip. Tactile shear is relevant to the contact, but the question is about distinguishing slip from localization drift through fusion. Treating one signal as a conclusive slip indicator would add an unsupported assumption.
Then could wheel–arm odometry by itself prove that the discrepancy is localization drift?

No such proof is specified for wheel–arm odometry either. It contributes information about the manipulator’s motion, but the question is whether that information, together with contact information in the proposed graph, can distinguish the two explanations while RGB-D is occluded.
What role does the contact anchor play if the contact itself may slip?

It makes the gripper–furniture relationship central to the estimation problem; it does not declare that relationship fixed. A contact-anchored graph that estimates slip can represent uncertainty about relative motion at contact. The open question is whether its available observations during a 3-second RGB-D occlusion can resolve that uncertainty separately from localization drift.
Is localization drift just another name for the furniture sliding?

No. Gripper–furniture slip concerns relative motion at their contact. Localization drift concerns error in the manipulator’s estimate of its position. Either could affect how the furniture’s position appears to be changing, which is precisely why the distinction matters.
Would an apparent mismatch between predicted and observed motion answer the question?

A mismatch would indicate that an expectation and an observation do not agree; by itself, it would not identify the cause. The question calls for telling gripper–furniture slip apart from localization drift, not merely noticing that something appears inconsistent during the occlusion.
Does the question require a decision before RGB-D returns, or could the distinction be made afterward?

Its wording asks whether fusion can distinguish the two *during* 3-second RGB-D occlusions. That makes the occluded interval central. It does not specify a decision deadline within those 3 seconds or say whether a later RGB-D observation may be used to assess what happened, so we should not add either condition.
Could we answer yes on the grounds that intermittent RGB-D was included in the proposal?

No. Inclusion of intermittent RGB-D does not establish what can be distinguished while RGB-D is occluded. Nor does listing tactile shear and wheel–arm odometry establish their performance during that interval. The question remains open on the information given.
Could we answer no simply because RGB-D is unavailable for those 3 seconds?

That would also be too strong. The proposed fusion has tactile shear and wheel–arm odometry as well as intermittent RGB-D. The absence of a new RGB-D observation during the occlusion poses a challenge, but it does not, by itself, prove that distinguishing slip from drift is impossible.
How does this relate to estimating furniture pose?

Furniture pose is another estimate in the proposed contact-anchored graph. The question focuses on whether two possible explanations for an apparent discrepancy—gripper–furniture slip and localization drift—can be separated during a 3-second RGB-D occlusion. Estimating furniture pose is part of that broader proposal, but a pose estimate alone would not demonstrate that the two explanations were correctly distinguished.
Is the 3-second interval a claim that the system has already handled occlusions of that length?
No. Three seconds specifies the RGB-D occlusion duration in the question. It is not a reported result, a guaranteed operating range, or evidence that the proposed fusion succeeds for that duration.
Would the 90% balanced-accuracy goal settle this specific question?

It states a desired level of slip-versus-localization-drift identification performance without external tracking during execution; it is not a measured result. It also does not, by itself, give performance specifically during 3-second RGB-D occlusions. The question asks whether the proposed contact-anchored fusion can make the distinction under that particular occlusion condition.
So what is the most careful answer right now?

It is not yet known from the stated information. Contact-anchored fusion of tactile shear, wheel–arm odometry, and intermittent RGB-D is the proposed approach, and a 3-second RGB-D occlusion poses a specific test of whether it can distinguish gripper–furniture slip from localization drift without a current RGB-D observation. No outcome for that test is provided.
Here is the hypothesis for that question: contact-frame tactile shear and wheel–arm residuals achieve ≥90% slip-versus-drift balanced accuracy during 3-second RGB-D occlusions.

That is a testable hypothesis, not a reported result. It predicts that contact-frame tactile shear and wheel–arm residuals can distinguish gripper–furniture slip from localization drift with at least 90% balanced accuracy under the specific condition of 3-second RGB-D occlusions. It does not establish that they already do so.
What does putting tactile shear in the contact frame add to the wording?

It specifies the frame in which the tactile-shear information is considered: the contact frame. That keeps the contact relationship central to the proposed distinction. The hypothesis does not define the contact-frame coordinates, a sensor design, or a particular calculation from the shear readings.
And what are wheel–arm residuals, at the level we can discuss here?

“Residuals” refers broadly to discrepancies associated with the wheel–arm motion information. The hypothesis identifies those residuals as information to use alongside contact-frame tactile shear, but it does not say exactly how they are computed or which model defines the discrepancy. We should not supply a specific residual equation as though it were part of the hypothesis.
Is the claim that tactile shear alone reaches ≥90%, and wheel–arm residuals alone do too?

No. The hypothesis names contact-frame tactile shear *and* wheel–arm residuals together. It predicts ≥90% slip-versus-drift balanced accuracy for their use in this setting; it gives no separate accuracy claim for either source alone.
Does ≥90% mean the same thing as exactly 90%?
No. “≥90%” means at least 90%: exactly 90% would meet the threshold, and a higher value would also meet it. The hypothesis does not predict one exact score.
Why say balanced accuracy instead of simply saying 90% of cases are classified correctly?

Balanced accuracy gives equal weight to recall for slip and recall for localization drift. For those two classes, it is the average of their recalls. A score of at least 90% balanced accuracy is therefore a different claim from at least 90% overall correctness, particularly if the classes are not equally frequent.
Does the hypothesis guarantee at least 90% recall for each class separately?
No. It sets a threshold for the average of the two class recalls. It does not separately impose a ≥90% threshold on both slip recall and localization-drift recall.
Are the 3 seconds an accuracy tolerance, or the length of the visual interruption?

They are the duration of the RGB-D occlusion. The accuracy threshold is ≥90% balanced accuracy. The hypothesis ties that classification threshold to the condition of a 3-second interruption in RGB-D observations.
Should I read this as a prediction about any visual occlusion, however long?
No. The hypothesis specifies 3-second RGB-D occlusions. It does not make the same performance claim for longer occlusions, shorter occlusions, or every possible form of visual unavailability.
Does it say the classifier has to announce slip or drift at every instant within those 3 seconds?

It says the distinction reaches ≥90% balanced accuracy *during* 3-second RGB-D occlusions. It does not define a per-instant reporting schedule or a deadline within the interval. Those details should not be inferred from the accuracy claim.
What exactly are the two things being distinguished?

The distinction is between gripper–furniture slip—relative motion at their contact—and localization drift—error in the manipulator’s position estimate. The hypothesis predicts that the named contact-frame shear and wheel–arm residual information can tell those apart during the stated occlusions; it is not merely a prediction that they can detect some unspecified discrepancy.
Could maintaining contact make the slip class contradictory?

No. The gripper and furniture can remain in contact while slipping relative to each other. Maintaining contact is consistent with a question about whether slip occurs at that contact, and the hypothesis concerns distinguishing that slip from localization drift.
Does this hypothesis say RGB-D observations are useless?

No. It concerns performance during a 3-second RGB-D occlusion, when a new observation from the occluded RGB-D view is unavailable. It does not claim that RGB-D is unhelpful when available, or revise the broader proposal to fuse intermittent RGB-D with tactile and motion information.
Can I say the contact-anchored graph has already achieved this score?

No. The current statement is a hypothesis about contact-frame tactile shear and wheel–arm residuals. It reports no evaluation outcome for those signals or for the contact-anchored graph. The ≥90% figure is the predicted balanced-accuracy threshold, not an observed score.
Does meeting this hypothesis automatically mean the furniture will be repositioned within 5 cm in 90% of trials?

No. The hypothesis concerns slip-versus-drift identification during 3-second RGB-D occlusions. Repositioning unseen furniture within 5 cm in 90% of trials under intermittent visual occlusion is a separate goal. Identification performance alone would not establish final-placement performance.
Is the 90% in the repositioning goal interchangeable with the ≥90% here?

No. The repositioning goal specifies success within a 5 cm placement tolerance in 90% of trials. This hypothesis predicts at least 90% *balanced accuracy* for distinguishing slip from drift during 3-second RGB-D occlusions. The percentages refer to different outcomes and different measures.
The broader goal excludes external tracking during execution. Does the hypothesis introduce external tracking to make its prediction?

It does not name external tracking. It names contact-frame tactile shear and wheel–arm residuals as the information supporting the predicted distinction during RGB-D occlusion. Nothing in the hypothesis should be expanded into an unstated external-tracking arrangement.
If a discrepancy appears during an occlusion, would that alone confirm the hypothesis?

No. Observing a discrepancy is not the same as correctly identifying whether it reflects gripper–furniture slip or localization drift. The hypothesis is specifically about the balanced accuracy of that distinction across the relevant cases, not simply noticing that expected and observed motion differ.
What is the careful one-sentence version, keeping its uncertainty intact?

The hypothesis is that contact-frame tactile shear and wheel–arm residuals can distinguish gripper–furniture slip from localization drift with ≥90% balanced accuracy during 3-second RGB-D occlusions; whether they actually achieve that performance remains unestablished here.

To investigate whether contact-anchored fusion can distinguish slip from localization drift during 3-second RGB-D occlusions, I plan to collect induced-slip and odometry-drift pushes, fit the contact-anchored fusion, and evaluate balanced accuracy across those occlusions on unseen furniture.

That gives the question a concrete evaluation plan. The induced-slip and odometry-drift pushes provide cases relevant to the two explanations being distinguished. Fitting the contact-anchored fusion is the proposed modeling step, and evaluating balanced accuracy across 3-second RGB-D occlusions on unseen furniture is the proposed assessment. None of those steps is described as completed.
Why collect both induced-slip and odometry-drift pushes?

Because the question is not just whether the system detects an unusual motion. It asks whether it can tell gripper–furniture slip from localization drift. Collecting pushes associated with each gives the planned evaluation both sides of that distinction. The plan does not specify how many pushes of either kind will be collected or how they will be induced.
Does “odometry-drift pushes” mean the furniture itself must slip during those pushes?

No. The phrase identifies pushes used to examine the localization-drift side of the distinction. It should not be taken to assert gripper–furniture slip in those pushes as well. The plan does not specify the exact motion or contact behavior in each collected case.
Is the collection step already evidence that the fusion can separate the two?

No. Collecting the pushes would provide material for fitting and evaluation; it would not itself establish classification performance. The balanced-accuracy evaluation is the planned way to assess the distinction, and no outcome is reported here.
What does “fit contact-anchored fusion” commit us to?

It commits the plan to fitting the proposed fusion approach, with contact as the organizing relationship for estimating the relevant motion and discrepancies. It does not specify a fitting algorithm, graph factors, parameterization, or sensor-processing rule. Those would be additional implementation details, not facts contained in this plan.
Should we explicitly say that the fit uses tactile shear, wheel–arm odometry, and intermittent RGB-D?

Those are the information sources named in the contact-anchored fusion proposal. Referring to that proposal identifies what “contact-anchored fusion” means here. This plan itself focuses on collecting the two kinds of pushes, fitting that fusion, and evaluating its slip-versus-drift balanced accuracy across 3-second RGB-D occlusions on unseen furniture.
Does evaluating across occlusions mean RGB-D is available throughout each 3-second interval?

No. The intervals are specifically 3-second RGB-D occlusions. The evaluation concerns how well the distinction is made in that condition, not performance under continuous RGB-D observation. The plan does not say exactly when observations are available before or after each occlusion.
Why keep the duration at exactly 3 seconds in the plan?

Because 3-second RGB-D occlusions are the condition in the question this plan addresses. Retaining that duration makes the proposed evaluation specific. It does not imply a result for other occlusion lengths or establish that the fusion works for 3 seconds.
What does “across 3-second occlusions” say about the timing of a classification?

It identifies the condition over which balanced accuracy is to be evaluated. It does not set a per-instant classification schedule, specify how many predictions are made per occlusion, or define a decision deadline within the three seconds. Those details remain unspecified.
Why evaluate on unseen furniture?

Unseen furniture is part of the stated evaluation condition. It prevents the plan from being described merely as an assessment on furniture already familiar to the fitted fusion. The plan does not define the particular furniture, the amount of prior exposure that counts as “seen,” or a specific division of collected cases.
Can I infer a particular training and test split from the words “fit” and “unseen”?

No particular split is specified. The plan distinguishes fitting from evaluating on unseen furniture, but it gives no allocation rule, dataset size, or procedure for ensuring that condition. Those details should not be presented as already decided.
Why use balanced accuracy for the evaluation rather than just report whether the pushes looked plausible?

Balanced accuracy directly addresses the two-way slip-versus-drift distinction. It averages recall for the slip class and recall for the localization-drift class, so it assesses recognition of both rather than merely whether some pushes appeared plausible. The plan names that metric but provides no measured value.
Does the plan set a balanced-accuracy result?
No. It says to evaluate balanced accuracy; it does not report a score or state that the fusion reaches a threshold. A planned measurement must remain distinct from its eventual outcome.
Would this evaluation also show whether furniture finishes within 5 cm of its intended placement?

Not as stated. This plan evaluates slip-versus-drift balanced accuracy across 3-second RGB-D occlusions on unseen furniture. It does not specify an evaluation of final furniture placement or a repositioning success rate. Those outcomes should not be inferred from the planned classification evaluation.
Does collecting odometry-drift pushes mean we have already determined how drift will be produced?

No. The plan names odometry-drift pushes as a category to collect, but does not give a mechanism, magnitude, or procedure for producing drift. Likewise, it does not specify how slip is induced in the induced-slip pushes.
Could we say the evaluation will identify exactly where every slip occurred?

That would go beyond the plan. Its stated evaluation is balanced accuracy for distinguishing slip from localization drift across the specified occlusions. It does not include a separate slip-location or slip-timing evaluation.
Do we need to claim an external tracking setup to make the evaluation meaningful?

The plan does not specify an external tracking setup or how reference classifications are obtained. The broader goal rules out external tracking during execution for slip-versus-drift identification. We should preserve that constraint without inventing an evaluation apparatus or claiming that one has already been selected.
So what is the careful formulation of the plan?

Collect induced-slip and odometry-drift pushes, fit the contact-anchored fusion, and evaluate its slip-versus-drift balanced accuracy across 3-second RGB-D occlusions on unseen furniture. That is a plan to investigate the distinction, not a completed evaluation or a performance claim.
The activity is to run OccludedPush-120 on unseen furniture, inducing either gripper slip or wheel-odometry bias during 3-second RGB-D blackouts, and measure balanced accuracy.

That specifies an evaluation activity for the slip-versus-drift distinction. OccludedPush-120 is the named run; unseen furniture is the object condition; induced gripper slip or wheel-odometry bias supplies the two conditions of interest; and each stated RGB-D blackout lasts 3 seconds. Balanced accuracy is the measure to obtain. The activity description does not report a score or say the run has been completed.
Does the “120” in OccludedPush-120 tell us how many pushes or furniture items there are?
Not on its own. OccludedPush-120 is the activity’s name, but no count of pushes, trials, or furniture items is stated separately. We should not turn the name into an assumed sample size.
What is the distinction between induced gripper slip and wheel-odometry bias here?

Induced gripper slip concerns relative motion at the gripper–furniture contact. Wheel-odometry bias concerns the motion estimate associated with the wheels, making it relevant to the localization-drift side of the distinction. The activity uses those as contrasting conditions; it does not specify their magnitudes or how either is induced.
Should we call every wheel-odometry-bias case a measured instance of localization drift?

The activity names wheel-odometry bias as the induced condition. It is pertinent to evaluating whether an apparent discrepancy is attributed to localization rather than gripper slip, but the wording does not provide measurements of the resulting drift. It is more precise to retain “wheel-odometry bias” when describing what is induced.
Does “or” mean both disturbances happen together in each push?

No. The activity says induced gripper slip *or* wheel-odometry bias. It does not state that both are induced together in every push. Nor does it specify how many cases of either kind the run contains.
What does calling the interruptions RGB-D blackouts add?

It makes the loss of RGB-D observations explicit for the stated 3-second intervals. Those blackouts are the condition under which slip-versus-drift balanced accuracy is to be measured. The activity does not specify exactly when the blackouts start relative to each push or what RGB-D observations are available outside them.
Is this a test of whether the contact-anchored approach works without any information at all during a blackout?

No. An RGB-D blackout removes that source of observations during the interval; it does not say all information is unavailable. The contact-anchored approach under discussion uses tactile and motion information as well. The activity does not, however, specify exactly which readings arrive at which moments in a blackout.
How does this activity bear on the ≥90% balanced-accuracy hypothesis?

Measuring slip-versus-drift balanced accuracy under 3-second RGB-D blackouts provides an evaluation relevant to the hypothesis that contact-frame tactile shear and wheel–arm residuals achieve ≥90% balanced accuracy under such occlusions. The activity supplies no measured accuracy, so it cannot yet establish whether that threshold is reached.
Why measure balanced accuracy instead of only counting correct labels?

Balanced accuracy treats the two classes symmetrically by averaging their recalls. That is relevant when measuring how well gripper-slip cases and the wheel-odometry-bias condition are distinguished. A raw count of correct decisions alone would not express the same class-balanced measure. No counts or class frequencies are given for OccludedPush-120.
Does the activity require at least 90% recall in each condition?

No such per-condition threshold is stated. The activity says to measure balanced accuracy. The associated hypothesis sets a ≥90% threshold for that average, not separate ≥90% recall requirements for each class.
Is unseen furniture important to the description of this run?

Yes. OccludedPush-120 is to be run on unseen furniture, so dropping that condition would make the activity less specific. The wording does not identify furniture types or define the exact prior exposure that qualifies an item as unseen.
Can we say the run evaluates how accurately the furniture is repositioned within 5 cm?

Not from this activity description. Its named measurement is balanced accuracy for the slip-versus-drift distinction during the specified blackouts. It does not state that final furniture-placement error or the percentage of successful repositioning trials is measured in this run.
Does running OccludedPush-120 mean the ≥90% score has been obtained?
No. “Run OccludedPush-120” states the activity to carry out, and “measure balanced accuracy” states what to assess. Neither wording supplies an observed value, whether above or below ≥90%.
Could we specify a camera setup or an external tracker to explain the blackouts?

The activity specifies 3-second RGB-D blackouts but not a camera arrangement or a tracking apparatus. Adding either would invent an implementation detail.
